humanities_role_explanation: MMLU's humanities subjects (including History, Philosophy, World Religions, Jurisprudence, and Ethics) are explicitly designed to test specialized disciplinary knowledge, factual accuracy, and subject-specific reasoning rather than using humanities materials as raw corpus data for general language modeling or linguistic tasks.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: A text-only multiple-choice question-answering format utilizing LaTeX for mathematical expressions and text-encoded questions/choices.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Tasks include multiple-choice QA testing factual recall of historical events and religious concepts, logical and deductive reasoning in formal logic, causal and temporal reasoning in world and US history, and normative judgment regarding moral scenarios and jurisprudence.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Evaluates LLMs across 57 distinct subjects spanning STEM, humanities, social sciences, and professional fields.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates GPT-3 (various sizes) and UnifiedQA (T5-based models) under zero-shot and few-shot paradigms.

quantitative_metrics.note: Evaluates models using multi-class classification accuracy (%) and root mean squared (RMS) calibration error.

published_after_march_2023.note: The paper was published at ICLR 2021, which predates March 2023.

summary: The paper introduces the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, composed of 15,908 multiple-choice questions across 57 academic and professional subjects. Evaluated primarily in zero-shot and few-shot settings, it shifts the focus of NLP benchmarking from basic commonsense or generic linguistic tasks to specialized, domain-specific academic knowledge. The authors demonstrate that while scale significantly improves performance, state-of-the-art models remain far below expert human levels and display highly lopsided domain capabilities.
key_findings: The largest GPT-3 model (175B) achieves an average few-shot accuracy of 43.9% (and UnifiedQA 11B achieves 48.9%), substantially above random chance (25%) but far short of the estimated human expert baseline (89.8%). Models show distinct performance drops on highly procedural/calculation-heavy tasks and socially critical value-aligned domains (such as law and ethics), alongside severe miscalibration (up to 24% discrepancy between model confidence and actual accuracy).
facets_explanation: The dataset consists of 15,908 multiple-choice questions gathered from standardized test preparation materials, university exams, and textbook resources, establishing pre-authored answer keys as the ground truth. Because these questions evaluate factual and academic knowledge in a closed-book format, correct answers require external domain knowledge not found in the prompt. Annotator divergence or alternative interpretations of the source questions are not addressed, as the benchmark relies directly on the absolute correctness of the source keys.
results_explanation: The paper reports a baseline for 'unspecialized humans' at '34.5% accuracy' and an 'expert-level accuracy' of 'approximately 89.8%'. The best-performing model evaluated is 'UnifiedQA' which 'attains 48.9% accuracy' (Table 1), resulting in an expert-to-model gap of 40.9 percentage points (rounded to 41). Although the paper notes that removing the '</s>' format token from UnifiedQA's inputs causes accuracy to decline 'by several percentage points' (Appendix A.3), it does not quantify this gap precisely, so no format gap is reported as an integer.
